y1: In those days, a wedding began at night with the bridegroom coming to the bride's house to take her. The bride's friends waited with lamps. It was unknown when the bridegroom would arrive.
y2: All ten girls fell asleep. The difference was not in staying awake, but in being 'prepared.' Oil could not be borrowed. Faith and preparation cannot be borrowed from someone else; they belong to each person.
y3: Traditionally, it is interpreted in various ways, such as the Holy Spirit, good deeds, or faith. If we connect it with 7:21–23, it is not just saying 'Lord, Lord,' but a life that does the will of the Father. The bridegroom's words 'I don't know you' are also the same as in 7:23.
y5: One talent was about 20 years' wages for a laborer. Even the servant who received the least received a huge amount. The master entrusted it 'to each according to his own ability.' The amount is different, but the expectation is the same.
y6: The servants who received five and two talents 'went at once' and traded. The servant who received one talent dug in the ground. According to rabbinic law at the time, burying money in the ground was the safest way against theft. His goal was not to lose it.
y7: The English word 'talent' (ability) comes exactly from this parable. But the talent in the parable is not just ability; it is everything God has entrusted to us: the Gospel, time, relationships, and opportunities.
y9: Two servants receive the same praise: 'Well done, good and faithful servant! You were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord!' It is not the size of the result that is praised, but the faithfulness.
y10: The third servant says: 'You are a hard man ... I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth.' A wrong idea about the master bred fear, and fear caused him to do nothing.
y11: There is no 'servant who lost money in business' in this parable. God regrets the one who was afraid and did nothing more than the one who tried and failed. A person who knows the God of grace can take the risk of failure and try.
y13: The Son of Man will come in His glory and separate all nations as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. Surprisingly, the criterion is not religious knowledge, but how they treated the hungry, the thirsty, the strangers, the naked, the sick, and those in prison.
y14: Both the sheep and the goats are surprised: 'Lord, when...?' Those who served did not know they were doing it to Jesus. Because they loved without calculating. Jesus identifies Himself with the least.
y15: This scene does not mean 'being saved by doing good works.' A person who receives the King's grace naturally loves the least of these. The fruit proves the root (7:17). The entire Gospel of Matthew speaks of a faith where word and deed are one.
verse: “The King will answer them, ‘Most certainly I tell you, because you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.’”
prayer: Jesus, thank You for teaching me that waiting is not standing still, but a time filled with love. Let me prepare the oil of faith that I cannot borrow from anyone else, and dig up the talent I buried in fear to use it faithfully. Let me see You in the face of the least of these and serve them. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: lamp. It was likely a torch made by wrapping oil-soaked cloth around the end of a stick. Oil had to be added every 15 minutes. This is the root of the word 'lamp'.
d1: talent. About 6,000 denarii. Even one talent was a huge sum of money that was hard to hold in a lifetime. It is the same unit as the ten thousand talents debt in 18:24.
d2: faithful. It shares the same root as the word 'faith' (pistis). Faithfulness is faith seen in action. 'Be faithful to death' (Revelation 2:10).
d3: least. It is connected to 'a cup of cold water to one of these little ones' in 10:42 and 'causes one of these little ones to stumble' in 18:6. Jesus comes looking for us in the face of the least of these.
